section_summary: This section consists chiefly of public and congressional appeals to halt American exports of scrap iron, steel, oil, aircraft, and other war materials to Japan during the Sino-Japanese War. State Department replies explain that the Neutrality Act would embargo arms to both China and Japan if invoked, did not authorize restrictions on scrap metal and similar commodities, and had been supplemented only by a policy discouraging aircraft exports to states bombing civilians. The section also includes British export and credit statistics, an internal statistical explanation disputing claims that the United States supplied 54.4 percent of Japan's total war materials, and a large California petition against shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of John H. Behlesser's letter on neutrality legislation
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Behlesser's advocacy of neutrality-law changes allowing selective embargoes against aggressor states.
subfiles.summary: The Department notes Behlesser's desire to empower the President to distinguish aggressors from nonaggressors and embargo war materials only to aggressor nations. Yost also thanks him for supporting the government's foreign policy.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Caroline J. Porter's protest against exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Richard B. Wigglesworth
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent's letter urging an end to scrap-iron, war-material, and credit exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Representative Wigglesworth encloses Caroline J. Porter's letter concerning shipments to Japan. He asks Secretary Hull for any comments the Department may wish to provide.

subfiles.title: Caroline J. Porter letter urging congressional action against Japan
subfiles.from: Caroline J. Porter
subfiles.about: Urges Congress to stop scrap iron, war materials, and war credits from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: Porter argues that American public sentiment opposes participation in Japan's war. She cites Japan's treaty violations and bombing of civilians as grounds for congressional action.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Wigglesworth on neutrality law and exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Explains the legal limits on stopping American exports to Japan and the consequences of invoking the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that a presidential finding of war would prohibit arms, ammunition, and implements of war to both China and Japan, while scrap iron was outside the statutory list. He reports licensed arms-export values since July 1937 and says the President acted within his discretion by not issuing a proclamation. Hull adds that the government condemned bombing civilians and directly discouraged aircraft and aeronautical-equipment exports to offending countries.

subfiles.title: British Embassy aide-mémoire on exports and credit to Japan
subfiles.from: British Embassy, Washington
subfiles.about: Reports British restrictions, exports of war material and steel, and diminishing private credit facilities to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The British Embassy says only six of eight arms-export licenses had been used since hostilities began, none for aircraft, and gives the total value of arms and naval stores exported to Japan. British steel exports to Japan had fallen sharply from 1937 to 1938, although no policy discouraged them. Financial institutions were already reducing short-term credit, while Japan could still use existing sterling resources.

subfiles.title: Calvary Baptist Church petition to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Woman's Missionary Society of Calvary Baptist Church
subfiles.about: Petitions the President to end American trade that supports Japanese military operations in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns Japan's invasion, treaty violations, bombing of cities, and killing of Chinese civilians. It denounces American supplies of planes, bombs, shells, scrap iron, oil, and trucks to Japan and asks for every practicable measure to end the traffic. It also offers future consideration of Japan's needs after withdrawal from Chinese territory.

subfiles.title: Calvary Baptist Church petition to Secretary Hull
subfiles.from: Woman's Missionary Society of Calvary Baptist Church
subfiles.about: A parallel petition asks the President and Congress to end American trade supporting Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: The society invokes the Nine-Power Treaty, Kellogg Pact, and Good Neighbor principle in condemning Japanese aggression. It asks for direct or indirect action against exports of raw materials and military supplies while leaving open assistance to Japan after evacuation of China.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Flossie G. Lyons
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the church society's petitions and explains the Neutrality Act and aircraft-export policy.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that recognizing a state of war would embargo arms to both China and Japan and that no statutory authority otherwise prevented such exports. He reports licensed-export values and notes that licenses for aircraft and supplies to countries bombing civilians had virtually ceased. Copies of the Neutrality Act and International Traffic in Arms were enclosed.

subfiles.title: George D. Wilder request for clarification of Japan war-material statistics
subfiles.from: George D. Wilder
subfiles.about: Requests data explaining the widely publicized claim that the United States supplied 54.4 percent of Japan's war materials.
subfiles.summary: Wilder says his impending return to Beijing will expose him to questions from Chinese acquaintances about American governmental and business conduct. He asks Hornbeck for manageable explanatory data and also appeals for support of the Church Committee for China Relief.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck explanation of the 54.4 percent statistic
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Distinguishes the American share of selected Japanese imports from the share of all materials used in Japan's military operations.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck explains that the 54.4 percent figure referred to American origin within a selected group of Japanese imports, not to Japan's entire consumption of war materials. He attributes the statistic to a Chinese economic study and notes Senator James P. Pope's use of related figures. Department estimates suggested that American imports represented considerably less than ten percent, perhaps seven percent, of Japan's total material expenditure, and Hornbeck asks not to be quoted as the source.

subfiles.title: White House transmittal of the Satterfield-Hughes petition correspondence
subfiles.from: M. H. McIntyre
subfiles.about: Forwards Congressman Satterfield's letter and a petition led by Jennie Hughes for acknowledgment.
subfiles.summary: McIntyre sends the State Department correspondence received by the President concerning exports of war materials to Japan. He asks that it be suitably acknowledged.

subfiles.title: Satterfield letter transmitting the Jennie Hughes petition
subfiles.from: Dave E. Satterfield Jr.
subfiles.about: Transmits a Richmond petition concerning exports of war materials to Japan for presidential consideration.
subfiles.summary: Representative Satterfield forwards a petition signed by Jennie Hughes and others. He asks that it receive appropriate consideration by the President.

subfiles.title: Petition to the President concerning exports of war materials to Japan
subfiles.from: Jennie Hughes and other petitioners; circulated by Margaret Monteiro
subfiles.about: Calls on the President to end American trade contributing to Japanese attacks on China.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns Japan as a treaty violator and protests bombing and killing of Chinese civilians. It lists American bombs, aircraft, shells, scrap iron, oil, and trucks supplied to Japan and asks Roosevelt to use every practicable means to stop the traffic.

subfiles.title: Edward H. Rees letter urging restrictions on scrap-metal exports
subfiles.from: Edward H. Rees
subfiles.about: Urges the National Munitions Control Board to prevent exports of iron and steel scrap to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Rees praises the government's effort to discourage aircraft exports to countries bombing civilians but argues that scrap metal is equally a raw war material. He cites large increases in American scrap exports to Japan during the undeclared war with China. He asks the National Munitions Control Board to adopt and enforce rules stopping the shipments.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Edward H. Rees
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Explains that existing law gave no agency authority to prohibit iron- and steel-scrap exports.
subfiles.summary: The reply says the Neutrality Act explicitly excluded raw materials such as iron and scrap steel from the arms category, even if the President recognized a state of war. It points Rees to prior Senate hearings and notes that comparable war-related commodities remained freely exportable. Although condemning attacks on civilians and defending the aircraft policy, the Department concludes that unilateral action against versatile scrap metal was not warranted without legal authority.

subfiles.title: Arthur E. Northey letter to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Arthur E. Northey
subfiles.about: Accuses the administration of enabling Japan's war by declining to recognize a state of war and stop material exports.
subfiles.summary: Northey argues that legal technicalities should not outweigh the lives of Chinese civilians or American ideals. He says citizens would support decisive action, praises credits to China, and invokes earlier American presidents as examples of moral leadership.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Arthur E. Northey
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains why the administration had not invoked the Neutrality Act against both belligerents.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that a war proclamation would halt arms exports to both China and Japan, while the Act did not cover other commodities. He supplies licensed-export totals and explains that aircraft licensing to states bombing civilians had virtually ceased. The Neutrality Act and an explanatory pamphlet were enclosed.

subfiles.title: Rupert Epworth League protest against munitions sales
subfiles.from: Margaret Moser, President, Rupert Epworth League
subfiles.about: Young church-league members urge immediate enforcement of neutrality legislation in the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.summary: The league contends that an unmistakable state of war exists in East Asia and protests munitions sales to the belligerents. It argues that raising relief funds for China while supplying Japan with instruments of war compromises American honor and friendship with China.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Margaret Moser
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Answers the Epworth League's demand for application of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that a presidential proclamation would embargo arms to China as well as Japan and that other commodities were beyond the law's scope. He gives licensed arms-export values and describes the effective cessation of aircraft licenses to countries whose forces bombed civilians. Copies of the relevant resolution and pamphlet were enclosed.

subfiles.title: Frank H. Ryder letter on American supplies to Japan
subfiles.from: Frank H. Ryder
subfiles.about: Praises Hull's trade policy but asks him to stop American arms, steel, oil, and other supplies from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ryder congratulates Hull for promoting international trade and goodwill. He nevertheless expresses shame and public disgust that American materials were assisting Japan's assault on China and asks whether the government could end the traffic.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Frank H. Ryder
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Thanks Ryder for supporting trade agreements and explains the statutory treatment of arms, steel, and oil exports.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that a Neutrality Act proclamation would embargo arms to both China and Japan. Steel, oil, and similar products were not defined as arms, and no existing statute authorized the President or Secretary of State to prohibit their export. He also supplies the Department's licensed arms-export totals.

subfiles.title: Kate H. Owing cover letter transmitting San Diego petitions
subfiles.from: Kate H. Owing, for the San Diego Peace Committee and local WILPF branch
subfiles.about: Transmits 1,001 additional signatures and another organizational protest against exports of scrap iron and war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Owing says approximately 5,000 signatures had already been sent to the Department on the issue. She argues that Congress should strengthen neutrality legislation to include all war materials or replace the existing law as ineffective. A communication from the Native Daughters and Native Sons is also enclosed.

subfiles.title: Native Daughters and Native Sons protest against scrap-iron exports
subfiles.from: San Diego Parlor No. 208, Native Daughters of the Golden West, and San Diego Parlor No. 108, Native Sons of the Golden West
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt and Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Protests scrap-iron and other war-material shipments to Japan and asks that scrap be placed on the prohibited list.
subfiles.summary: The organizations describe every pound of exported scrap iron as potential material for killing and maiming civilians. In the interests of peace and security from aggression, they request enforcement of neutrality laws and the addition of scrap iron to the banned list.

subfiles.title: Mass petition against shipment of scrap iron and war materials to Japan
subfiles.from: San Diego Peace Committee petitioners and other California signers
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt and Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Thousands of petitioners protest American shipments of scrap iron and other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Each sheet repeats the demand that the President and Secretary of State stop shipments of scrap iron and other war materials to Japan. The surviving pages contain large numbers of handwritten names and addresses, chiefly from San Diego County but also from other California communities and a few places outside the state. Many signatures are only partly recoverable because of handwriting and OCR degradation.
